results.question: A thesis shows a music-generation model uses 30% less energy at similar quality on benchmark prompts. Why is that not yet evidence of a successful product?

options.text: Energy savings never matter to customers
options.explanation: They might matter a lot. The point is that a benchmark alone does not show it.

options.text: Thesis results are usually wrong
options.explanation: The result can be perfectly good. It just answers a different question.

options.text: Models cannot be turned into products
options.explanation: They can, but the product is the model plus the rest of the system.

options.text: A benchmark result answers a research question; a product must give a customer something they value, reliably, at a price the business can sustain
options.explanation: Right. The gap is everything around the model: measurement, reliability, updates, cost and responsibility.

results.correctAnswer: A benchmark result answers a research question; a product must give a customer something they value, reliably, at a price the business can sustain
workedSolution: The thesis result is about a model on a fixed set of prompts.
A product has to answer whether a customer gets something they value every time, at a sustainable price.
Most of the open questions are not about the model: accuracy that customers care about, availability, updating and rollback, cost, unacceptable mistakes, privacy.
The model is one component, and most of the product is everything else.

results.question: In machine-learning systems, where does the specification of correct behaviour mostly come from?

options.text: From the compiler
options.explanation: A compiler does not supply behaviour.

options.text: From rules a programmer writes down and tests
options.explanation: That is traditional software. For ML the rules are learned rather than written.

options.text: From the training data, so a change in the data can change behaviour even if no code changed
options.explanation: Right. This is inductive rather than deductive: behaviour follows from the data seen, so the data is part of the program.

options.text: From the model architecture alone
options.explanation: The architecture matters, but the behaviour is learned from data.

results.chosenAnswer: From the training data, so a change in the data can change behaviour even if no code changed
results.correctAnswer: From the training data, so a change in the data can change behaviour even if no code changed
workedSolution: Traditional software: deductive, you write the rule and a test that it holds.
Machine learning: inductive, the model generalises from observations.
Its behaviour follows from the data it saw, so no written spec exists and black-box behaviour is hard to check.
Changing the data can change the behaviour with no code change: the data is part of the program.

results.question: What does “correct” realistically mean for a model's output?

options.text: Every prediction matches the specification
options.explanation: There is usually no specification to match, and no model achieves this.

options.text: It works well enough, on average, on some test data, so a system must tolerate some wrong predictions
options.explanation: Right. An average score tells you how often you are wrong, not how badly or where.

options.text: It is fast
options.explanation: Speed is a separate quality from correctness.

options.text: It passes every unit test
options.explanation: Unit tests can check rules, but models do not follow written rules.

results.chosenAnswer: It works well enough, on average, on some test data, so a system must tolerate some wrong predictions
results.correctAnswer: It works well enough, on average, on some test data, so a system must tolerate some wrong predictions
workedSolution: There is no rule to check each output against.
You can only measure whether it works well enough, on average, on test data.
Some individual predictions will be wrong, and the average does not say which or how badly.
So the design question becomes: what happens when it is wrong, and how bad is that?

results.question: A data scientist is typically judged on accuracy on evaluation data. A software engineer is typically judged on what?

options.text: Accuracy on evaluation data, the same as a data scientist
options.explanation: That is the data scientist's usual measure.

options.text: Number of models trained
options.explanation: This is an output, not a measure of success.

options.text: Model size only
options.explanation: Model size is one of the things data scientists often ignore, not the engineer's main measure.

options.text: Customer satisfaction, through performance, stability and release time
options.explanation: Right. Trouble starts when each role assumes the other's concerns are the same as its own.

results.chosenAnswer: Customer satisfaction, through performance, stability and release time
results.correctAnswer: Customer satisfaction, through performance, stability and release time
workedSolution: Data scientist: a fixed dataset, judged by accuracy, prototyping in notebooks.
Software engineer: large live data, judged by customer satisfaction, maintaining and extending over time.
Neither is wrong: an undeployable model is not a product and a product around a poor model is not useful.
Friction comes from optimising for different things without realising it.

results.question: What is the difference between a T-shaped and a π-shaped person?

options.text: Both have breadth across many areas; T-shaped has one deep area, π-shaped has two, typically a technique and a domain
options.explanation: Right. Breadth lets you collaborate; depth lets you contribute.

options.text: T-shaped people are generalists with no depth
options.explanation: The stem of the T is deep expertise in one area.

options.text: π-shaped people are deep in every area
options.explanation: π has two deep areas, not all of them.

options.text: They describe seniority: T is junior and π is senior
options.explanation: They describe the shape of one's skills, not career level.

results.chosenAnswer: Both have breadth across many areas; T-shaped has one deep area, π-shaped has two, typically a technique and a domain
results.correctAnswer: Both have breadth across many areas; T-shaped has one deep area, π-shaped has two, typically a technique and a domain
workedSolution: The horizontal bar is breadth and the vertical stems are depth.
T-shaped: broad, with one deep area (for example deep neural networks).
π-shaped: broad, with two deep areas, naturally a technique and a domain such as medical systems.
Depth makes you useful; breadth makes you useful to a team.

results.question: Which of these is characteristic of scientists rather than computer scientists, as the course contrasts them?

options.text: They are comfortable that data has errors and nothing is ever completely true or false
options.explanation: Right. With data you weigh evidence and expect it to be imperfect.

options.text: They build their own clean, organised virtual worlds
options.explanation: That describes computer scientists.

options.text: They test algorithms on random data
options.explanation: That is the habit the lecture ascribes to computer scientists.

options.text: They invent rather than discover
options.explanation: The lecture attributes “invent rather than discover” to computer scientists.

results.chosenAnswer: They are comfortable that data has errors and nothing is ever completely true or false
results.correctAnswer: They are comfortable that data has errors and nothing is ever completely true or false
workedSolution: Scientists: study a messy natural world, data-driven, obsessed with discovering, comfortable with errors.
Computer scientists: build clean virtual worlds, algorithm-driven, invent, and expect everything to be true or false.
With data, rigour means working out how far to trust it and saying how sure you are.

results.question: “Genius shows in finding the right answer. Wisdom shows in avoiding the wrong answers.” Why does the course say data science benefits more from wisdom?

options.text: Wrong answers are rare in data science
options.explanation: The lecture argues the opposite: they are easy to make and hard to notice.

options.text: Genius is not needed at all
options.explanation: Genius has value, but it benefits less than wisdom.

options.text: An analysis can produce a clean-looking wrong answer without any error message, and you cannot always check it against the truth
options.explanation: Right. The protection is the habit of doubting your own result before someone else does.

options.text: Data scientists are hired to produce code
options.explanation: The lecture says software developers are hired to produce code and data scientists to produce insights.

results.chosenAnswer: An analysis can produce a clean-looking wrong answer without any error message, and you cannot always check it against the truth
results.correctAnswer: An analysis can produce a clean-looking wrong answer without any error message, and you cannot always check it against the truth
workedSolution: Insights are claims about the world, and the world does not tell you when you are wrong.
A bug crashes something; a mislabelled column or skewed sample produces a tidy but wrong chart.
Since you cannot always check against the truth, you build the habit of asking how you might be wrong.
Wisdom comes from experience, general knowledge, listening to others and humility.

results.question: You use a baseball dataset to ask “Do left-handed people have shorter lifespans than right-handed people?” What is the main caution?

options.text: Professional ballplayers are not a random sample of people, so the data may not stand in for the wider population
options.explanation: Right. Each step away from what the data describes raises the question of who is missing.

options.text: Left-handedness is always recorded incorrectly
options.explanation: Nothing suggests this. The problem is who is in the data.

options.text: Baseball data does not contain any dates
options.explanation: It records each year's statistics, so dates are present.

options.text: Questions about people cannot be asked of sports data
options.explanation: They can, but the stretch from players to people needs care.

results.chosenAnswer: Professional ballplayers are not a random sample of people, so the data may not stand in for the wider population
results.correctAnswer: Professional ballplayers are not a random sample of people, so the data may not stand in for the wider population
workedSolution: A dataset's subject is the thing it describes: players and teams.
Using it as a stand-in for people in general stretches it.
Professional ballplayers are selected, so conclusions about the population may not hold.
Ask who is missing before generalising.

results.question: In the Google Ngrams data, the frequency of a word rises sharply after 1990. Which is the most careful reading?

options.text: The data is useless for any question
options.explanation: It is very useful, provided you check it against the biases of the corpus.

options.text: It might reflect a real change, but also more books being printed or more recent titles being scanned, so check the corpus first
options.explanation: Right. Counts in a corpus describe the corpus; whether they describe the world depends on how it was assembled.

options.text: The word became more popular, with certainty
options.explanation: That is one possibility, but the corpus itself may have changed.

options.text: Ngrams cover every book ever published
options.explanation: The lecture says it covers about 15% of all books.

results.chosenAnswer: It might reflect a real change, but also more books being printed or more recent titles being scanned, so check the corpus first
results.correctAnswer: It might reflect a real change, but also more books being printed or more recent titles being scanned, so check the corpus first
workedSolution: Ngrams counts words in scanned books, about 15% of books ever published.
A rise in a word's frequency could mean the world changed, or that more books were printed, or that recent titles are over-represented in the scan.
Counts in a corpus describe the corpus.
Whether they describe the world depends on how the corpus was assembled.

results.question: Which of these taxi-data questions cannot be answered by looking things up in the records, and needs an answer to be built?

options.text: “How many trips were taken in total?”
options.explanation: This is a count of records, a lookup.

options.text: “What is each driver's total fare on a given night?”
options.explanation: Nearly a lookup: sum the fares by driver and night.

options.text: “Where should drivers go to pick up their next fare?”
options.explanation: Right. The record does not contain the answer; you must build it from the rest and decide how far to trust it.

options.text: “Where do people travel to and from at different times of day?”
options.explanation: This is close to a lookup: pickup and dropoff locations and times are in the records.

results.chosenAnswer: “Where should drivers go to pick up their next fare?”
results.correctAnswer: “Where should drivers go to pick up their next fare?”
workedSolution: Locations, times and fares are recorded, so travel patterns and nightly totals come from the records.
“Where should a driver go next?” is a recommendation. It is not stored anywhere.
You have to build a model from the other data and then decide how far to trust it.
That is where data science begins.

results.question: A classifier claims to output probabilities for three mutually exclusive outcomes. Which set of scores could be a valid probability distribution?

options.explanation: They add to 1.2, but the probabilities of all outcomes must add to 1.
They add to 1, but a probability cannot be negative.
They add to 0.9, so an outcome is missing or a number is wrong.
Right. Each is between 0 and 1 and they add to 1.

workedSolution: Rule 1: each `p(s)` satisfies `0 ≤ p(s) ≤ 1`.
Rule 2: the probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1.
`0.5 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 1.0` and all are in range.

results.question: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25. Are A and B independent?

options.text: Yes, since 0.25 is below both P(A) and P(B)
options.explanation: Being below each is true of any intersection. It does not test independence.

options.text: It cannot be decided without the sample size
options.explanation: The product rule uses the probabilities you already have.

options.text: No: independence needs P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.20, but the observed value is 0.25
options.explanation: Right. Here B makes A more likely: P(A|B) = 0.25/0.4 = 0.625, above P(A) = 0.5.

options.text: Yes, since the probabilities are all reasonable numbers
options.explanation: Independence is a numerical claim, checked by the product rule.

results.chosenAnswer: No: independence needs P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.20, but the observed value is 0.25
results.correctAnswer: No: independence needs P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.20, but the observed value is 0.25
workedSolution: Independent means `P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B)`.
Observed `P(A ∩ B) = 0.25 ≠ 0.20`, so they are not independent.

results.question: Roll two fair dice and learn that the first die is a 5. What is the probability that the total is 10 or more?

options.explanation: Right. Of the six outcomes (5,1) to (5,6), two reach 10: (5,5) and (5,6).
That is 2/36, the joint probability. Conditioning divides by P(first die is 5) = 6/36.
That would be the answer if the first die were a 6. With a 5, only two outcomes reach 10.
That is the unconditional probability, 6/36. You have been told something that raises it.

workedSolution: Condition on `B`: the first die is 5. Six equally likely outcomes remain, `(5,1)` to `(5,6)`.
The total is at least 10 for `(5,5) = 10` and `(5,6) = 11`.
Unconditionally `P(A) = 6/36 = 1/6`, so the information raised it.

results.question: A condition affects 2% of people. A test detects it in 95% of those who have it, but wrongly flags 10% of those who do not. You test positive. Roughly what is the probability you have the condition?

options.text: About 16%
options.explanation: Right. Out of 10,000 people, 190 true positives and 980 false positives give 190/1170 ≈ 16%.

options.text: About 95%
options.explanation: That is P(positive | condition), the number the test makers report. You need P(condition | positive).

options.text: About 2%
options.explanation: That is the prior. The positive result should raise it.

options.text: About 90%
options.explanation: That would ignore the base rate. When the condition is rare, false alarms outnumber true ones.

results.chosenAnswer: About 16%
results.correctAnswer: About 16%
workedSolution: Picture 10,000 people. `2%` have it: 200. `98%` do not: 9,800.
True positives: `0.95 × 200 = 190`. False positives: `0.10 × 9,800 = 980`.
Total positives `190 + 980 = 1,170`.
`P(condition | positive) = 190 / 1,170 ≈ 0.162`. The base rate dominates.

results.question: Let V be the sum of two fair dice. What is the cumulative probability F(9) = P(V ≤ 9)?

options.explanation: That is P(V ≥ 10). It is the complement of the right answer.
Right. The counts for totals 2 to 9 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, which sum to 30.
That is P(V = 9), the height of one bar. F(9) adds all bars up to and including 9.
That is P(V ≤ 8). The bar at 9 must be included.

results.question: A chart shows cumulative iPhone sales climbing steeply, and someone concludes growth is exploding. What is the flaw?

options.text: A running total always rises, even at constant sales; the growth rate is the incremental change, which is better shown by plotting sales per period
options.explanation: Right. Choose the plot for the question: cumulative curves show totals to date, not how fast things are changing.

options.text: Cumulative charts cannot show sales at all
options.explanation: They show totals to date correctly. They just do not show the rate.

options.text: Steep curves are always caused by outliers
options.explanation: A steep cumulative curve can come from perfectly steady sales.

options.text: The cdf and pdf carry different information
options.explanation: They hold exactly the same information. The problem is what is easy to see by eye.

results.chosenAnswer: A running total always rises, even at constant sales; the growth rate is the incremental change, which is better shown by plotting sales per period
results.correctAnswer: A running total always rises, even at constant sales; the growth rate is the incremental change, which is better shown by plotting sales per period
workedSolution: A running total never goes down.
Selling the same number every quarter still makes the cumulative line rise.
Rate of growth is the derivative of that curve, which is hard to judge by eye.
Plot sales per period instead.

results.question: A histogram of phone prices uses $50-wide bins. The bar for $200–$250 has a density of 0.004 per dollar. How much probability is in that bar?

options.explanation: Right. The probability in a bar is its area: height × width = 0.004 × 50.
This multiplies by 5 rather than 50.
This is the density multiplied by 1000, not by the width.
That is the density, not the probability. You need to multiply by the bin width.

workedSolution: For a histogram, height is a density: probability per unit of `x`.
`P(bar) = height × width = 0.004 × 50 = 0.2`.
Rebinning into $100 bins would keep the density near 0.004 but hold 0.4 in each bar.
With width 1 the multiplication changes nothing, which is the rule for the dice.

results.question: Salaries in a small company are 50k, 50k, 60k, 70k and 5M. Which measure best describes a typical salary, and why?

options.text: The median, 60k, because an outlier controls the mean but barely touches the median
options.explanation: Right. The mean is about 1.05M, which describes nobody.

options.text: The mean, about 1.05M, because it uses every value
options.explanation: It does use every value, but that is exactly why one outlier drags it away from the typical salary.

options.text: The geometric mean, because these are ratios
options.explanation: These are amounts, not ratios or growth rates. The median is better for skewed data.

options.text: Any of them, since they are all called “the average”
options.explanation: They can differ by a factor of twenty here, so which one you report matters.

results.chosenAnswer: The median, 60k, because an outlier controls the mean but barely touches the median
results.correctAnswer: The median, 60k, because an outlier controls the mean but barely touches the median
workedSolution: Median: sort and take the middle value, 60k.
Four of five people earn under 71k, so the median describes the group and the mean does not.
Skew and outliers favour the median.

results.question: An investment gains 100% in year 1 and loses 50% in year 2. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It ends where it started; the geometric mean of the multipliers 2 and 0.5 is 1, whereas the arithmetic mean of the percentages (+25%) is misleading
options.explanation: Right. Multipliers compose by multiplication, so growth is averaged with the geometric mean.

options.text: It lost 50% overall
options.explanation: The second-year loss of 50% applies to the doubled amount, which returns it to the start.

options.text: It gained 25% overall, the average of +100% and −50%
options.explanation: Start with 100: it becomes 200, then 100. Nothing was gained.

options.text: It gained 100% overall
options.explanation: That ignores the second year's loss.

results.chosenAnswer: It ends where it started; the geometric mean of the multipliers 2 and 0.5 is 1, whereas the arithmetic mean of the percentages (+25%) is misleading
results.correctAnswer: It ends where it started; the geometric mean of the multipliers 2 and 0.5 is 1, whereas the arithmetic mean of the percentages (+25%) is misleading
workedSolution: Multipliers: `2` and `0.5`.
Geometric mean of multipliers: `√(2 × 0.5) = √1 = 1`, so no net change.
Arithmetic mean of the percentages: `(100 − 50)/2 = +25%`, which is wrong.

results.question: The values 1, 3, 5, 7 are the whole population. What is the (population) standard deviation?

options.explanation: That divides by n − 1, which is the sample formula. With the whole population you divide by n.
Right. Mean 4, squared distances 9, 1, 1, 9 sum to 20, variance 20/4 = 5, and SD = √5.
That is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.
That is the sum of squared distances, before averaging or square-rooting.

workedSolution: Squared distances: `9, 1, 1, 9`, which sum to `20`.
Population variance: `20 / 4 = 5`. SD: `√5 ≈ 2.24`.
Dividing by `n − 1 = 3` would give the sample SD `√6.67 ≈ 2.58`.

results.question: A player whose true batting ability is exactly 0.300 hits 0.275 over 500 at-bats. What should you conclude?

options.text: Their ability has clearly declined
options.explanation: A 0.275 season is well within the ordinary variation for a 0.300 hitter.

options.text: Nothing about their ability: a season like that happens by chance about one time in nine
options.explanation: Right. Each observed value is one draw from a distribution. About 0.02 is the natural wobble of the average, so 0.275 is only around 1.2 deviations low.

options.text: They were unlucky, and luck is impossible to estimate
options.explanation: The size of luck can be estimated with a standard deviation, which is the point of the example.

options.text: The measurement must be wrong
options.explanation: The number is fine. It is simply a noisy draw.

results.chosenAnswer: Nothing about their ability: a season like that happens by chance about one time in nine
results.correctAnswer: Nothing about their ability: a season like that happens by chance about one time in nine
workedSolution: For 500 at-bats at a 30% rate, the observed average has a standard deviation of about `0.02`.
`0.275` is `0.025 / 0.02 ≈ 1.2` standard deviations below `0.300`.
That is ordinary wobble: 11% of seasons are 0.275 or lower.
Before explaining a difference, ask how big a difference chance alone could produce.

results.question: Model B scores 0.5% higher accuracy than the simpler Model A on a single train/test split. What does the course recommend?

options.text: Treat the gap as possibly noise, measure the noise (for example by repeating the evaluation), and prefer the simpler model unless B clearly beats the variation
options.explanation: Right. Choosing simple when scores are indistinguishable gives interpretability, speed and less overfitting at no measured cost.

options.text: Discard both models
options.explanation: There is no reason to do that. Measure the noise instead.

options.text: Choose B, since higher is always better
options.explanation: A small gap can come from which split was chosen or how parameters were optimised.

options.text: Choose whichever model is more complex
options.explanation: Complexity has to earn its place with a gain clearly bigger than noise.

results.chosenAnswer: Treat the gap as possibly noise, measure the noise (for example by repeating the evaluation), and prefer the simpler model unless B clearly beats the variation
results.correctAnswer: Treat the gap as possibly noise, measure the noise (for example by repeating the evaluation), and prefer the simpler model unless B clearly beats the variation
workedSolution: Differences can come from the split chosen, from how well parameters were optimised, and other accidents of the process.
A 0.5% gap is like a hitter moving from 0.300 to 0.302.
Measure the noise, for example with repeated splits.
If the gap is not clearly larger than the noise, take the simpler model.

results.question: Which of these is a legitimate way to reduce variance in an evaluation?

options.text: k-fold cross-validation: evaluate on k different splits and average
options.explanation: Right. Repeating the experiment steadies the estimate, and you can see the spread as well.

options.text: Delete test examples the model gets wrong
options.explanation: That is dishonest. Outliers may be removed only with a good reason, which you must explain.

options.text: Use one split and increase the number of digits reported
options.explanation: More digits do not make the estimate any less noisy.

options.text: Report only the best of several runs
options.explanation: That reports a lucky draw and hides the variation.

results.chosenAnswer: k-fold cross-validation: evaluate on k different splits and average
results.correctAnswer: k-fold cross-validation: evaluate on k different splits and average
workedSolution: The listed methods: pick the lower-variance option, repeat the experiment (such as k-fold cross-validation), sample properly, and remove outliers only if justifiable.
Averaging over `k` splits reduces dependence on one lucky split.
Dropping inconvenient points to improve the score is not justified.
Reporting the best run overstates the result.

results.question: Two printer-cartridge suppliers both advertise a mean life of 3000 pages. Supplier A's lifetimes have SD 100 and Supplier B's have SD 800. You need every cartridge to last at least 2500 pages. What does this show?

options.text: They are equivalent, since the means are the same
options.explanation: Same mean, different behaviour: this is exactly the trap.

options.text: The mean alone is not enough: A's tight spread makes it the safer choice, because B produces many short-lived cartridges
options.explanation: Right. A buyer planning stock cares about the spread at least as much as the average.

options.text: Nothing can be said without the median
options.explanation: The SD already tells you that A's values cluster and B's do not.

options.text: B is better because a higher SD means higher quality
options.explanation: A higher SD means more variation, which here means unreliable lifetimes.

results.chosenAnswer: The mean alone is not enough: A's tight spread makes it the safer choice, because B produces many short-lived cartridges
results.correctAnswer: The mean alone is not enough: A's tight spread makes it the safer choice, because B produces many short-lived cartridges
workedSolution: The mean says where the distribution sits. The SD says how wide it is.
A: 2500 is 5 SDs below the mean, so short-lived cartridges are very rare.
B: 2500 is only 0.6 SDs below the mean, so a large share falls short.
Same mean, different reliability. Mean and SD together describe a distribution fairly well.

results.question: Delivery times have a mean of 60 s and a variance of 16 s², with unknown shape. At least what fraction of deliveries take between 48 and 72 seconds?

options.text: About 89%
options.explanation: Right. σ = 4, so 48 to 72 is 60 ± 12, which is k = 3 standard deviations, and Chebyshev guarantees at least 1 − 1/9 ≈ 0.89.

options.text: About 75%
options.explanation: That is the guarantee for k = 2. The interval here is 3 standard deviations wide on each side.

options.text: No guarantee can be given
options.explanation: That is what k = 0.75 would give, from mistaking the variance 16 for σ. Take the square root first.

options.text: About 95%
options.explanation: That is the normal distribution's figure for 2 sigma, which needs a bell-shaped distribution.

results.chosenAnswer: About 75%
results.correctAnswer: About 89%
workedSolution: Variance is 16, so `σ = √16 = 4`.
Chebyshev: at least `1 − 1/k² = 1 − 1/9 ≈ 0.89` lies within `k` sigma.
Using the variance as σ would give `k = 12/16 = 0.75` and no useful bound.

results.question: A colleague says “about 95% of any data lies within two standard deviations of the mean.” What is the problem?

options.text: Chebyshev guarantees 99% for two standard deviations
options.explanation: For k = 2 it guarantees 1 − 1/4 = 75%.

options.text: No fraction can be guaranteed for any data
options.explanation: Chebyshev gives a guarantee for every distribution with a mean and standard deviation.

options.text: Nothing, it is a general rule
options.explanation: The 95% figure belongs to the normal distribution.

options.text: That is true only for roughly normal data; without knowing the shape, Chebyshev guarantees only 75% within two standard deviations
options.explanation: Right. Chebyshev is loose because it must hold for every distribution, but that is what makes it a safe fallback.

results.chosenAnswer: That is true only for roughly normal data; without knowing the shape, Chebyshev guarantees only 75% within two standard deviations
results.correctAnswer: That is true only for roughly normal data; without knowing the shape, Chebyshev guarantees only 75% within two standard deviations
workedSolution: Chebyshev: at least `1 − 1/k²` of the mass lies within `k` standard deviations.
Normal data has about 95% there, because it is a tamer shape.
When you cannot vouch for the shape, use the guarantee that holds for all of them.

results.question: For X = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and Y = X², Y is completely determined by X. What is Pearson's r?

options.explanation: Nothing about the arrangement suggests a partial positive linear trend. The products cancel exactly.
Right. The left half votes negative, the right half votes positive, and they cancel: r measures only straight-line relationships.
There is no straight-line decrease either.
That would need Y to rise in step with X in a straight line.

workedSolution: A perfect dependence with zero linear correlation.

results.question: For X = 1, 2, 3 and Y = 2, 1, 3, what is Pearson's r?

options.explanation: The points are not on a straight line.
The sign is positive, because the point with the largest x also has the largest y.
The products do not cancel: they sum to 1.
Right. The covariance sum is 1, and the denominator is √2 · √2 = 2.

workedSolution: Distances: `X − X̄ = −1, 0, 1` and `Y − Ȳ = 0, −1, 1`.
Products: `0, 0, 1`, sum `1`. Squares: `Σ(X − X̄)² = 2` and `Σ(Y − Ȳ)² = 2`.

results.question: Every X value is multiplied by 1000 (a change of units, say metres to millimetres). What happens to the covariance and to Pearson's r?

options.text: Both grow a thousandfold
options.explanation: The denominator grows by the same factor as the numerator, so r cancels the change.

options.text: The covariance grows a thousandfold and r does not change
options.explanation: Right. The denominator divides out each variable's spread, so r is unit-free and always in [−1, 1].

options.text: r becomes larger than 1
options.explanation: r is always between −1 and 1, whatever the units.

options.text: Both stay the same
options.explanation: The covariance grows with the units. It determines the sign but not the scale.

results.chosenAnswer: The covariance grows a thousandfold and r does not change
results.correctAnswer: The covariance grows a thousandfold and r does not change
workedSolution: Numerator: `Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ)` gets multiplied by 1000.
Denominator: `√Σ(X − X̄)²` gets multiplied by 1000 as well.
Covariance alone cannot compare relationships in different units; r can.

results.question: Two variables have a correlation of r = −0.7. What share of the variance in Y is explained by X?

options.explanation: That is |r|. The share of variance explained is r², which is smaller.
This divides by 10 rather than squaring.
A share of variance cannot be negative. The sign of r is only direction.

options.text: About 49%
options.explanation: Right. r² = 0.49. The sign gives the direction and does not matter for variance explained.

results.correctAnswer: About 49%
workedSolution: For simple linear regression, `R² = r²`.
So about 49% of the variance in `Y` is explained.
Because of the square, predictive value decreases quadratically: `r = 0.3` explains only 9%.

results.question: With n = 10,000 data points, a correlation of r = 0.03 is found to be statistically significant. What is the right reading?

options.text: A significant result must be an important one
options.explanation: Large samples make small correlations significant. Significance says nothing about size.

options.text: r must be recomputed with a bigger sample
options.explanation: The sample is already large. The issue is what the effect means.

options.text: The relationship is probably real, but it explains under 0.1% of the variance, so it is unlikely to matter on its own
options.explanation: Right. Significance measures whether an effect is real; effect size (r²) measures whether it is big enough to matter.

options.text: The result is spurious, since r is small
options.explanation: With 10,000 points even r ≈ 0.02 counts as significant. It is probably real.

results.chosenAnswer: The relationship is probably real, but it explains under 0.1% of the variance, so it is unlikely to matter on its own
results.correctAnswer: The relationship is probably real, but it explains under 0.1% of the variance, so it is unlikely to matter on its own
workedSolution: At `n = 10,000` the smallest significant `r` is about 0.02, so 0.03 passes.
Significance means the relationship is probably not chance.
Effect size: `r² = 0.03² = 0.0009`, under 0.1% of the variance.
Ask both questions: is it real, and is it big enough to matter?

results.question: Hours studied: 2, 3, 5, 8, 40. Marks: 50, 55, 61, 70, 72. What is Spearman's ρ?

options.explanation: Every rank difference is zero, so ρ is at the maximum.

options.text: Below 1, because of the outlier
options.explanation: Ranks cap how far an outlier can pull. It is just rank 5.
Marks rise every time hours rise, so there is a perfect monotonic relationship.
Right. Both variables have ranks 1 to 5 in the same order, so every rank difference is 0. The 40-hour outlier does not matter, because only order counts.

results.chosenAnswer: Below 1, because of the outlier
workedSolution: Pearson would be pulled below 1 by the point at 40 hours; Spearman sees only that more hours always came with a higher mark.

results.question: For x = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and y = 1, 3, 2, 5, 4, what is Spearman's ρ = 1 − 6Σd² / (n(n² − 1))?

options.explanation: That needs all rank differences to be 0, but y is not in the same order as x.
This would need Σd² = 16.
This would need Σd² = 12.
Right. The rank differences are 0, −1, 1, −1, 1, so Σd² = 4 and ρ = 1 − 24/120.

results.question: When is Spearman's rank correlation a better choice than Pearson's?

options.text: When the sample is very small
options.explanation: Sample size does not decide the choice. The shape of the relationship does.

options.text: When you want to measure causation
options.explanation: Neither measures causation.

options.text: When the relationship is consistently rising or falling but curved, when there are outliers, or when the data is only ordinal
options.explanation: Right. Pearson asks how straight; Spearman asks how ordered.

options.text: When the relationship is exactly a straight line
options.explanation: Pearson is well suited to that, and Spearman would give the same answer here.

results.chosenAnswer: When the relationship is consistently rising or falling but curved, when there are outliers, or when the data is only ordinal
results.correctAnswer: When the relationship is consistently rising or falling but curved, when there are outliers, or when the data is only ordinal
workedSolution: Spearman replaces values by ranks, so any steady rise or fall scores highly.
Ranks cap the pull of outliers, since the biggest value is just rank `n`.
It also works for ordinal data, such as satisfaction ratings.
Pearson looks for a straight line, so it suits linear relationships without extreme values.

results.question: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated across months. Which explanation fits best?

options.text: Ice cream causes drowning
options.explanation: Nothing plausible links eating ice cream to drowning.

options.text: Drowning causes ice-cream sales
options.explanation: The reverse arrow is equally implausible.

options.text: The correlation must be a mistake in the data
options.explanation: Hot weather explains it without any error.

options.text: A third factor, hot weather, drives both
options.explanation: Right. Whenever A and B correlate, name the reverse arrow and the third factor before believing a causal story.

results.chosenAnswer: A third factor, hot weather, drives both
results.correctAnswer: A third factor, hot weather, drives both
workedSolution: The four explanations: `A` causes `B`; `B` causes `A`; a common cause `C`; or pure coincidence.
Hot weather increases both ice-cream sales and swimming, which increases drownings.
Correlation is useful for prediction, but acting on it needs a causal claim.
Randomised experiments break the link to hidden third factors.

results.question: Daily sales show high autocorrelation at lags 7, 14 and 21, and near zero at lag 1. What does this suggest?

options.text: An upward trend
options.explanation: A trend correlates a series with itself at every lag, which drowns out cycles rather than giving peaks at 7, 14, 21.

options.text: Random noise
options.explanation: Noise would show no autocorrelation at any lag.

options.text: That sales cause the calendar
options.explanation: A peak is a pattern, not a cause.

options.text: A weekly cycle: the series resembles itself seven days earlier, but not the day before
options.explanation: Right. Peaks in the autocorrelation function mark cycle lengths, and multiples of the cycle also match.

results.chosenAnswer: A weekly cycle: the series resembles itself seven days earlier, but not the day before
results.correctAnswer: A weekly cycle: the series resembles itself seven days earlier, but not the day before
workedSolution: Autocorrelation at lag `k` correlates `S[t]` with `S[t + k]`.
High values at 7, 14 and 21, and a value near 0 at 1, mean today resembles the same weekday, but not yesterday.
That is a 7-day cycle.
A trend would need removing first, or it would inflate every lag.

results.question: Rainfall at station 1 “Granger-causes” rainfall at station 2 because a storm system passes over 1 first and 2 later. What does this show about the test?

options.text: The test can only be used for rainfall
options.explanation: It applies to any pair of time series.

options.text: It shows Granger causality is about prediction: timing is real but the arrow can be borrowed from a third factor, and it says nothing about direct versus indirect causes
options.explanation: Right. It upgrades “moves together” to “moves first”, a better clue than plain correlation, though still not proof.

options.text: Station 1's rain physically produces station 2's rain
options.explanation: The storm system is the real cause. Station 1's rain merely comes first.

options.text: The test proves causation whenever it is significant
options.explanation: It is a forecasting statement, weaker than the everyday meaning of cause.

results.chosenAnswer: It shows Granger causality is about prediction: timing is real but the arrow can be borrowed from a third factor, and it says nothing about direct versus indirect causes
results.correctAnswer: It shows Granger causality is about prediction: timing is real but the arrow can be borrowed from a third factor, and it says nothing about direct versus indirect causes
workedSolution: Granger: `Y` Granger-causes `X` if the past of `Y` improves prediction of `X` beyond the past of `X` alone.
Here the storm `C` reaches station 1 first and station 2 later.
Past rainfall at 1 helps predict 2, yet neither causes the other.
It is a stronger clue than correlation, not a substitute for an experiment.

results.question: A model scores a document by multiplying the probabilities of its 500 words, each about 0.001. Working in base-10 logs, what is the log of the document's probability?

options.explanation: The probabilities are below 1, so their logs are negative.
Right. Each word contributes log₁₀(0.001) = −3, and 500 × −3 = −1500. The product 10⁻¹⁵⁰⁰ would underflow to zero in ordinary floating point.
Each word contributes −3, and 500 × −3 = −1500, not −150.
That is the log for a single word. There are 500 of them, and logs of products add.

workedSolution: `log(ab) = log a + log b`, so the log of the product is the sum of the logs.
Each word: `log₁₀(0.001) = −3`.
The raw product `10⁻¹⁵⁰⁰` is far below the smallest float, about `10⁻³⁰⁸`, so it underflows to 0 while the log sum is fine.

results.question: A price goes from 80 to 20. What is log₂ of the ratio new/old, and what does it show?

options.explanation: That would be log₂ of 1/16. 20/80 = 1/4.
That is the percentage change. The question asks for the log of the ratio.

options.text: 0.25, which is already symmetric
options.explanation: The raw ratio 0.25 is squeezed into 0 to 1, while a fourfold rise would be 4. It is not symmetric.

options.text: −2: a fall to a quarter of the price is the mirror image of a rise to four times (+2)
options.explanation: Right. Taking logs of ratios gives equal displacement for doubling and halving, and a ratio of 1 sits at 0.

results.chosenAnswer: −2: a fall to a quarter of the price is the mirror image of a rise to four times (+2)
results.correctAnswer: −2: a fall to a quarter of the price is the mirror image of a rise to four times (+2)
workedSolution: The reverse move, `20 → 80`, has ratio 4 and `log₂ 4 = +2`.
Averaging the raw ratios of a rise and a fall gives a lopsided answer; averaging the logs gives 0.

results.question: A typical student has about $10³ and a billionaire about $10¹¹. Someone with about $10⁶ is how far from each on a log₁₀ scale?

options.text: 10³ from the student and 10¹¹ from the billionaire
options.explanation: Those are the raw amounts. Distances on the log scale are differences of exponents.

options.text: 6 from each
options.explanation: 6 is the person's own position on the scale. The distances are differences of positions.

options.text: 3 above the student and 5 below the billionaire
options.explanation: Right. On the log scale the positions are 3, 6 and 11. Logs measure proportions, and each step is a factor of ten.

options.text: Exactly halfway between them
options.explanation: Halfway on the log scale would be 10⁷. At 10⁶ they are not equidistant.

results.chosenAnswer: 3 above the student and 5 below the billionaire
results.correctAnswer: 3 above the student and 5 below the billionaire
workedSolution: Positions on the `log₁₀` scale: student `3`, person `6`, billionaire `11`.
Distance to the student: `6 − 3 = 3` steps up.
Distance to the billionaire: `11 − 6 = 5` steps down.
Power-law data spans orders of magnitude, so analyse it on a log scale, where equal ratios are equal distances.
